What activated on Jan 1 was the EO that modified the Uniform Code of Military Justice. Those modifications are a bit complicated, but one of them was to allow civilian lawyers to augment military courts martial.

I've seen a number of posts claiming that it pertains to military tribunals. That may be partly true in that I believe the modifications also deal with how people will be handled at GITMO.

However, military tribunals are not governed by the UCJM. Instead, they are governed by the Military Commissions Act of 2009 which was an update from previous such acts to address Supreme Court rulings that found portions of the previous acts regarding military tribunals to be unconstitutional.

A military tribunal or commission is usually used to refer to a court that asserts jurisdiction over persons who are members of an enemy army, are held in military custody, and are accused of a violation of the laws of war. In contrast, courts-martial has jurisdiction only over members of the US military.

A military tribunal or commission may use the rules and procedures of a court-martial, although that is not generally the case. In a clarifying directive, the Secretary of Defenses stated that military tribunals should use the UCMJ as a "guideline" but are mostly governed by the Military Commissions Act of 2009.

Military tribunals also, generally speaking, do not assert jurisdiction over people who are acknowledged to be civilians who are alleged to have broken civil or criminal laws. However, tribunals can have jurisdiction over civilians who in time of war or rebellion commit such crimes as treason, sedition, crimes against humanity, spying, violating the laws of warfare, and a few others; but it is very limited.

The bottom line appears to be remanded to a military tribunal, the violation must be associated with a specific war or rebellion.

Today, we have the war on terrorism, the Korean War (we are technically still in a state of war with NK), Afghanistan, and Iraq. Any violations that occurred during previous conflicts such as Libya could also be tried by tribunals because there is no statute of limitations on treason, sedition, spying, crimes against humanity, etc.

There will be tribunals at GITMO. It didn't get a major upgrade for the 40 or so prisoners who are still there. But unless there is some sort of secret legal directive (perhaps the State Secrets Act) that changes the public criteria for military tribunals, only those who match the criteria will face a tribunal. The rest will be tried in civil court or military members who are charged but don't merit a tribunal will face courts martial.
